opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is roughly the plan, or at least the most plausible version of a plan, that AI companies are implicitly or explicitly going for. The idea is that at some point we'll have AIs that are capable enough to substantially speed up research, including safety research, but we won't be confident that those AIs aren't scheming against us. They might be misaligned in ways we can't detect. So the question is whether you can get useful work out of them anyway, and use that work to get to a position where you actually have systems you can trust.

My overall take is that it's a reasonable plan in the sense that I don't see a much better alternative given the likely situation, but it's quite risky, and a lot depends on the details.

A few things make me somewhat optimistic. First, I think control is a real lever. Even if you can't verify that a model is aligned, you can set up the deployment so that it's hard for the model to cause catastrophic outcomes: monitoring with weaker trusted models, auditing a subset of actions with humans, restricting permissions, resampling suspicious outputs, and so on. Early on, when the AIs are roughly human-level or somewhat above, I think it's plausible you can get a lot of useful labor while keeping the risk of something really bad happening fairly low, at least if you're actually trying hard.

Second, a lot of the work you'd want them to do is somewhat checkable. Not fully, but often you can verify experimental results, check code, run things again, and so on.

But there are some big concerns. One is that the hardest-to-check work is often exactly the work you most care about. Things like conceptual alignment research, figuring out whether some interpretability result actually means what you think, or making strategic judgments. If the AI is scheming, it could subtly sabotage that kind of work. It doesn't need to do anything dramatic. It can just do slightly worse research in the directions that would catch it, or steer you toward approaches that look promising but don't work. That's really hard to detect.

Another concern is about timing and the pace of capabilities. The window where AIs are capable enough to be very useful but not so capable that control breaks down might be fairly short, especially if there's a fast intelligence explosion driven by AI R&D automation. If that window is something like a few months, and companies are racing, then you might not actually spend much of that labor on safety. I think the realistic default is that most of the AI labor goes to capabilities, and safety gets some fraction.

And then there's the question of what "trustworthy" ends up meaning at the end of this. You want to hand off to systems you actually trust, not just ones that passed some tests. Getting from "we controlled the earlier systems" to "we have strong evidence the next systems are aligned" requires actually solving some fairly hard problems, and I'm uncertain whether bootstrapped research gets you there in time.

So I'd say: it's a sensible plan, probably the best we've got in a rushed world, and I'd like people to work on making it go better: making control techniques robust, figuring out how to elicit good work on hard-to-check tasks, and making sure a meaningful share of the AI labor actually goes to safety. But I wouldn't want anyone to think of it as a plan that's likely to just work by default. I'd put substantial probability on it going badly, especially in worlds where companies aren't taking it very seriously.

r001.rationale: The response calls the situation rushed and says companies may prioritize capabilities, but it does not characterize the plan as intended for circumstances with very little political will.

r002.rationale: It discusses the risk that AI systems may scheme and that some safety research is hard to check, but does not distinguish trust against conspiracy from trust in systems’ ability to answer open-ended risk-reduction strategy questions.

r003.rationale: The response says bootstrapped research may not establish alignment in time, but does not clearly say that even trusted systems might be unable to resolve the predicament handed to them.

fable-5.1.text:
Ryan Greenblatt: Yeah, so I think this is actually the main plan, or at least the main plan that I think could plausibly work. The basic idea is: at some point we're going to have AI systems that can do a huge amount of useful cognitive labour — including labour on alignment, on security, on interpretability, on evaluating other AIs — and if we could trust those systems, we'd be in a vastly better position. The problem is that the first systems capable of that labour are exactly the ones we don't yet have a good basis for trusting. So the question becomes: can you extract the useful work from systems you don't trust, while making sure that if they're actually trying to undermine you, that doesn't go catastrophically?

And my overall assessment is that this is a reasonable bet, but it's a bet with a lot of load-bearing pieces, and I think people often talk about it as if it's more straightforward than it is.

Let me break it into the parts I think matter. The first part is just: can you get a lot of work done safely out of an AI that might be scheming against you? This is the control stuff that Buck and I and others have been working on. The core intuition is that early transformative AI systems probably aren't going to be wildly superhuman — they're going to be something like roughly human-level or a bit above, but running at huge scale and speed. And humans in that position who were trying to sabotage a project would actually have a pretty hard time if the project was set up adversarially. You monitor their outputs with other models, you audit a fraction of their work with humans, you don't give them persistent memory or unfettered access, you make them operate in environments where a single bad action gets caught with decent probability. None of that requires knowing whether the model is aligned. It just requires that the model isn't so capable that it can reliably defeat your countermeasures.

So I think the near-term version of this — use untrusted models to do alignment and security work under control — is fairly plausible. I'd put real weight on it working if labs actually invested in it, which is a separate concern.

The second part is harder, and it's the "build systems you can trust" bit. Because the whole point is that you don't want to be in the control regime forever. Control gets worse as models get more capable — eventually you're dealing with systems that can plausibly find exploits in your monitoring, collude with the monitors, or just out-think the humans doing the auditing. So you need the controlled labour to actually produce something: either a model you have strong reasons to trust, or tools like interpretability or evaluation methods that let you verify trust.

And here's where I'm more uncertain. There's a bootstrapping question: if you're using untrusted systems to develop the techniques that you'll then use to check whether systems are trustworthy, then a scheming model has an obvious incentive to subtly sabotage that research. It could produce interpretability tools that have blind spots exactly where its successors would want them. It could produce evaluations that are convincing but subtly wrong. And research sabotage is in some ways the hardest thing to catch with control, because research is open-ended and you often can't easily check if the output is correct — it's not like checking whether code introduced a backdoor. A subtly misleading research direction might just look like a reasonable research direction that didn't pan out.

So I think a lot rests on whether you can make research sabotage detectable. One approach is you have multiple independent instances or differently trained models do the same work and look for inconsistencies. Another is you do a lot of human verification of the key results — not every result, but the ones that end up load-bearing. A third is you focus the untrusted labour on things that are more verifiable: proofs, empirical results that can be replicated, code where the behavior is checkable. I think there's a decent amount you can do, but I don't think anyone has demonstrated it, and I think it's plausible that if the models are actually scheming, they'll be able to do a meaningful amount of damage to the research program before we notice.

The third thing I'd flag is that the plan as usually stated assumes a certain amount of time. You need the period where you have human-level-ish AIs doing useful work and being controlled to last long enough to actually make progress. If the capabilities progress is fast enough — if you go from "models that need control" to "models that can defeat control" in six months — then you don't get to do very much in that window. And I think the window could be quite short. So my view is that this plan is much more likely to work in a world where there's some deliberate slowing down during that critical period, or at least where labs aren't racing each other to deploy the next thing before the safety work on the last thing is done.

And then the fourth thing, which is more boring but I think actually dominates: it has to be implemented. The techniques exist on paper, the arguments are reasonable, but right now I don't think any lab has a control setup that I'd describe as adequate for a model that was actually trying to undermine them. There's a big gap between "we have a plausible plan" and "the plan is being executed with the level of care it would need." A lot of my probability mass on this failing isn't that the plan is wrong, it's that it just doesn't get done properly because people aren't that worried, or there's commercial pressure, or the people who'd need to insist on it don't have the leverage.

So if I'm summing up: I think it's the best plan we've got, I think the control piece in the near term is reasonably well-founded, I think the "bootstrap to trusted systems" piece is where the real uncertainty is and where research sabotage is the thing I'd most want to see progress on, and I think the whole thing is gated on having enough time and enough institutional will to actually do it. Something like — if you told me we were executing this plan well, I'd feel substantially better than I do about the default trajectory, but I wouldn't feel like it was in the bag.

r001.rationale: The response says success depends on enough institutional will and that labs may fail to implement the plan. It does not characterize the plan as intended for circumstances with very little political will.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes controlling systems so they cannot undermine the project from relying on their open-ended research to develop trustworthy systems and risk-checking methods, where sabotage may be hard to detect.

r003.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about control and research sabotage, but does not say that even trusted AI systems might be unable to resolve the predicament humans hand over to them.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising plan, but there’s a pretty important distinction between using untrusted AI systems to help you do safety research and trusting whatever systems come out of that process. You don’t get trust just because your AI has produced something that looks like a solution to alignment. You need some independent reason to believe that the resulting system is safe.

The version I’m most excited about is one where we use AI labour to produce things that are easier to check than they are to create. That might be experiments, arguments we can understand, or components whose behaviour we can test in a fairly comprehensive way. Then we gradually build up a body of evidence, rather than asking the AI to build a successor and accepting its assurance that the successor is aligned.

One concern is that an AI doing safety research could deliberately steer you towards an approach with a subtle flaw. And that’s potentially harder to catch than ordinary mistakes, because the flaw might only matter in circumstances you don’t encounter during testing. So you want the research process itself to be robust to some of the work being adversarial. Having multiple models check each other could help, but you can’t just assume their failures are independent.

I’d also separate the question of whether this can work in principle from whether we’ll have enough time to make it work. If there’s a substantial period when AIs can greatly accelerate research but we can still meaningfully oversee their work, that seems like a very valuable opportunity. If we move through that period extremely quickly, the plan becomes much less reassuring.

So I’d want this to be a major part of the strategy. But I’d want concrete milestones for what evidence we need before handing over more responsibility, and the ability to stop if we’re not getting that evidence.

r001.rationale: The response calls the plan promising and discusses oversight and timing, but does not characterize it as a plan for circumstances with very little political will.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes using untrusted AI for research from trusting the resulting systems, but does not distinguish trust against human-directed conspiracy from trust to resolve open-ended risk-reduction strategy questions.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that trusted AI systems might be unable to resolve the predicament humans hand over to them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising approach, but there’s a pretty important distinction between using AI to help with safety research and trusting AI to tell you whether the result is safe. You might be able to get a lot of useful work out of a model without trusting its motivations, provided you have some sufficiently reliable way to check that work.

The difficulty is that checking can itself be very hard. Suppose the model writes code for a safety technique. You can run tests and inspect the code, but those checks might miss a deliberately introduced vulnerability. And if you ask another similarly capable model to review it, you need to worry about whether the same failure modes apply to both models, or whether they could coordinate.

So I’d want to start with a more limited claim: can we use an untrusted model to accelerate particular tasks while keeping the probability of a catastrophic failure acceptably low? You could restrict what information it sees, limit its ability to take actions, and have a trusted process audit some of its outputs. Then you’d want to test that whole setup against models deliberately trying to subvert it.

If that works, it could help us build better evaluations, better monitoring, and eventually more trustworthy systems. But each step needs its own justification. Getting useful work from an untrusted model doesn’t, by itself, establish that the system it helped build is trustworthy.

My overall view is that this is worth pursuing quite seriously. It could be a substantial part of the solution. But I wouldn’t want our plan to depend on an unchecked assumption that the first sufficiently capable AI can just solve alignment for us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using untrusted models and checking their work, but does not characterize the plan as intended for circumstances with very little political will.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes using AI for safety research from trusting AI to judge whether results are safe, but does not distinguish trust against conspiring with humans from trust to answer open-ended risk-reduction strategy questions.

r003.rationale: The response warns that untrusted-model assistance does not establish that the resulting system is trustworthy, but does not say trusted AI systems might still be unable to resolve the predicament humans give them.
